summary: Fort Point Light, a nine-sided iron tower on the brick fort under the Golden Gate Bridge: lit 1855 to 1934, now a National Park Service site.

light.characteristic: Changed over time: fixed white (1855); fixed white with a red flash each minute (1878); alternating red and white flashes (1903); white, 1 s on and 1 s off (1912).

lens.note: Order disputed: fourth (archive) or fifth (1972 report, LighthouseFriends, NPS).

structures.type: nine-sided iron tower on the fort's stairway
structures.note: Built 1863, lit January 1864. LighthouseFriends gives 28 ft. Wikidata's 8.2 m is unsupported by the sources read.

staffing.note: Keepers until the light went out on 1 September 1934.

access.note: Open to the public as a National Park Service site. LighthouseFriends: visitors can reach the top of the fort where the lighthouse is mounted, but are not allowed inside the lighthouse; grounds open, tower closed.

facts.agency: National Park Service (Golden Gate National Recreation Area)

events.note: First tower, built under the contract; never lit
Army tore down the unlighted tower in September 1853
Second tower on a ledge below the fort. Dates: 1 Feb (NPS), 21 Mar (1972 report), March (LighthouseFriends)
Fifth-order lens per the 1972 report and LighthouseFriends; the archive says fourth order
Light moved from the seawall to the top of the fort
Present iron tower built on the fort (archive: 1863)
Light in its new position apparently exhibited January 1864
Fourth of July salute fired from the fort damaged the fog-signal structure and machinery
Wooden bridge from the bluff to the fort (1972 report: built 1874; LighthouseFriends: 1876)
Fifth-order fixed white becomes fourth-order fixed white, varied each minute by a red flash
Fog bell exchanged with the large bell at Yerba Buena Island (1972 report, PDF p.23); LighthouseFriends describes the bell as 3,000 pounds.
Two keepers' dwellings on the bluff
Tramway with hand-operated winch built for supplies
City of Rio de Janeiro sank near Fort Point in fog (22 February 1901)
New fourth-order lens; alternating red and white flashes five seconds apart
Daboll trumpet atop the fort. LighthouseFriends: operating from 30 September 1904; 1972 report (PDF p.26): first used 1 October 1904.
Earthquake: little damage to the tower; bridge pulled southward (1972 report); LighthouseFriends: bridge slightly displaced
New head keeper's dwelling at the base of the bluff
New lens: white, 1 s on and 1 s off

Keeper James Rankin swam to help a man from an overturned boat, on 15 June. The Bulletin item gives no year (issue dated March 1913); the dated item printed beside it is from 1912, so 1912 is probable.
Rankin rescued a boy who had fallen from the sea wall (29 December 1918)
Rankin rescued another boy from the sea wall (6 January 1919)
Work on the Golden Gate Bridge began
Light discontinued 1 September 1934; the Golden Gate Bridge's north pylon stood outside the fog signal and light
Designated a National Historic Site, 16 October 1970 (LighthouseFriends). The 1972 report (PDF p.5) dates President Nixon's signing of the authorizing act to 19 October 1970.
National Park Service historic structure report on the light (Koue and Holland)

wrecks.outcome: Struck a rock ledge just offshore in fog and sank. The San Francisco Call gives a loss of 122 lives; the Lighthouse Board gives over 100. The board said an efficient fog signal might have prevented it.

keepers.name: Ephrain Sohn
keepers.note: Spelled 'Ephrain Sohn' in the 1972 table, appointed 1 April 1856 with no end date. Not in the archive roster.

corrections.why: The 1855 tower was on a ledge below the fort and was removed in 1863. The present iron tower was built on the fort in 1863 and lit in January 1864 (archive: tower established 1863; 1972 report; NPS).

resolved_conflicts.explanation: Wikidata's 1864 and the archive's 1855 are both right for different towers. The first light on the point was lit in 1855 on a ledge below the fort. The present tower dates from 1863, and the light was first shown from it in January 1864.

The archive records a fourth-order Fresnel lens in 1855. The 1972 report (quoting the 1859 Light List and a description of the 1850s) and LighthouseFriends give a fifth-order lens. The 1972 report also says the 1864 lantern was of the fourth order, which may explain the archive's entry. This is an inference and is flagged as such.

notes_for_editor: PAGES: the 1972 report's printed page numbers are not legible in the OCR, so every HSR footnote gives the PDF page. The keeper table lines (Appendix B, PDF pp. 55-56) are OCR'd and were matched by position: 'Scott Blanchard' (1 Sept 1864, table) is taken as the archive's 'Lott Blanchard' (1864-1866); 'J. c. Frachey' as the archive's 'J. C. Frackey'; the dates for Mary Thompson and Sophie Huie were matched by row order. Verify those three with the page image. The archive's 1853-1854 entries (James Rogan, Sarah Rogan, Charles Gilman, Heman Doyle) predate the lit second tower (lit March 1855); neither source explains them, and the story does not explain them. UNRESOLVED: (1) height of the light: 81 ft above mean high water (archive), 83 ft (LighthouseFriends), 166 ft above the water (1871 Light List as quoted in the 1972 report), and Wikidata's focal height 34.0 m (about 111 ft), which no source read supports; the 1871 Light List is not in the corpus. (2) First lighting date: 1 Feb 1855 (NPS web page), 21 March 1855 (1972 report), March 1855 (LighthouseFriends). (3) Bridge to the fort: 1874 (1972 report) or 1876 (LighthouseFriends).
